intro: To reopen a closed tab in Chrome on Mac, press ⌘ Shift T. Chrome brings back closed tabs in the order you closed them, so press it again to reach older ones.
tldr: Press ⌘ Shift T to reopen the tab you closed last.
Press it again for each older tab. Chrome works backward through the list.
If the shortcut does nothing, click Chrome first, then open More > History > History.
Desktop History covers the last 90 days. Incognito pages are not in it.

blocks.text: What this guide covers

This guide is for Google Chrome on a Mac running macOS Ventura or later. Chrome has the largest share of desktop browser use. StatCounter puts it at 66.98% of worldwide desktop browser share for October 2026, with Safari at 7.83%. If you use Safari, check Safari's own menus, because the names there are different.
Every shortcut and menu path below comes from Google's help pages, unless the text says otherwise. Where a step rests only on a third-party guide, the page says so.
Reopen a closed tab with ⌘ Shift T
Click any part of the Chrome window so it is the front app. Then press ⌘ Shift T. Hold Command and Shift, then tap T. Chrome reopens the tab you closed most recently.

Google's keyboard shortcuts page lists this combination for reopening previously closed tabs on Mac. The page gives the rule in one line: the tabs come back in the order they were closed. The newest closed tab returns first, and older tabs follow one at a time.
You do not need a menu, a search box, or a mouse. Your hands can stay on the keyboard, which is why it is worth learning before you need it.
Reopen several closed tabs in order

Each press brings back one tab. If you closed three tabs in a row, you need three presses to reach the first one you closed. Here is a worked example. You close a shopping cart page, then a news story, then a recipe.

Press ⌘ Shift T once and the recipe comes back. Press again and the news story returns. One more press brings back the shopping cart. Nothing else needs to happen, and you do not need to pick the tab yourself.

Many people press the shortcut once, see one tab, and assume the rest are gone. They are not gone yet. Keep pressing until the page you want appears. Watch the tab strip after each press, so you know which page came back.
If you lose track of how far back you went, keep count in your head or on a sticky note. Stop when you reach the page. It is easy to overshoot by a press or two and end up with a tab you do not want.
What happens when a whole window closed

Closing a whole window works the same way, one tab per press. Chrome restores the tabs in the order they closed, so the last tab in that window returns first. Google's shortcut page does not list a separate key for a closed window.

If several windows closed, keep pressing ⌘ Shift T until the window you want appears. A window full of tabs takes many presses. That can be slow, so the History page is often the better choice. It lists pages by time and title, and you can click the one you need.
Open History when the shortcut does nothing
Sometimes ⌘ Shift T seems to do nothing. One likely cause is that another app is in front, so the keys go there instead of to Chrome. Click the Chrome window and press the shortcut again.
If no tab comes back, use History. Click More, the three-dot button at the top right of the Chrome window. Choose History, then History again in the submenu. The History page opens in a new tab.
Google's help page also says that typing @history in the address bar searches your history. Use that when you remember a word from the page title but not the date.
Use ⌘ Y to open History faster
Google's shortcut page lists ⌘ Y as the key that opens History on Mac. The page opens in a new tab, so the tab you are working in stays put. Use it when you want the full list, not just the last tab.
Here is a simple rule. Use ⌘ Shift T when the page was open a moment ago. Use ⌘ Y when you remember a topic, a site, or a word from the title.
Find a tab you closed days ago in History

Desktop History covers the last 90 days. Anything older is not in the list. Chrome's History also leaves out chrome:// pages, Incognito pages, and pages you deleted from history. Synced pages from other devices where you are signed in do appear.

Say you closed a flight search last week. Open History and type the airline or the city in the search box at the top of the page. Look for the entry with the date and time you need, then click it to open the page again.
If the search returns too many results, add a second word from the page title. A narrower search makes the right entry easier to spot.
If the search returns nothing, the page may be older than 90 days, or it may have been an Incognito page. Check those two causes before you assume the page is gone for good.
Pages that will not come back

items: Incognito pages. They do not appear in History, so plan to bookmark anything you want to keep.
chrome:// pages, such as Chrome's own settings pages. History leaves them out.
Pages you deleted from history, or removed with Delete browsing data.
Anything older than 90 days on desktop.

blocks.text: Incognito needs its own note. Open a new Incognito window with ⌘ Shift N, or choose New Incognito window from the More menu at the top right. Close it with Close at the top left. The Incognito session ends when all Incognito windows are closed, so save anything you need before you close the last one.
Mistakes people make with closed tabs

items: Pressing ⌘ Shift N by mistake. That opens an Incognito window, not a closed tab. Close it with Close at the top left and try ⌘ Shift T again.
Expecting one press to bring back a whole window. Each press returns one tab.
Searching only the address bar and giving up. Type @history in the address bar, or open the History page for the full list.
Clearing history to tidy up. That removes entries you might need later.
Waiting too long to look. Desktop History covers the last 90 days, so older pages need a different plan, such as a bookmark.

blocks.text: Clear browsing data without losing your safety net

Deleting browsing data is the other thing that removes closed pages from History. On desktop, select More, then Delete browsing data. Choose a time range, check Browsing history, and select Delete data. The time range can be All time.

blocks.title: Check the time range
blocks.text: Choosing All time removes every entry in History, not only the one you want to find. Clear data only when you are sure you no longer need a recent page.
For the full walkthrough, read [how to clear browsing data in Chrome on Mac](/how-to/clear-browsing-data-in-chrome).
Other tab shortcuts worth learning
Google's shortcut list includes several tab keys that pair well with ⌘ Shift T. Start with the two you will use most, then add the rest when you need them.

items: ⌘ Option with the Left or Right arrow moves between tabs.
⌘ 1 to ⌘ 8 jump to a tab by position, and ⌘ 9 jumps to the last tab.

blocks.text: Menu items some guides mention

Some third-party guides describe a Reopen Closed Tab item in a File menu or a Recently closed submenu. Google's help pages do not document either one for Mac, so the steps in this guide avoid them. If your Chrome shows an item like that, you can try it. The shortcut and the History page are the routes Google documents.
Check your Chrome version if the shortcut behaves oddly

Chrome updates itself in the background. Google says updates normally happen when you close and reopen the browser. A new update ships about every four weeks, according to Google's Chrome download page.

Wikipedia lists 157.0.8103.39 as the stable desktop release for Windows and macOS, dated 3 November 2026. It also lists macOS Ventura or later as the supported system. Google's own release post did not show that version number when this page was checked on 9 November 2026, so treat the number as a Wikipedia figure.
To see your version, choose More > Help > About Google Chrome. If your number is older than the one listed, restart Chrome so any pending update can apply, then test the shortcut again.
Next steps after you reopen the tab
Once the tab is back, decide whether you need it again. If you keep losing pages, bookmark them as soon as they matter, so you do not depend on History later.

The [Incognito guide](/how-to/open-an-incognito-window-in-chrome) shows both ways to open a private window. If you want Chrome to open your links, read [how to set Chrome as default browser on Mac](/how-to/set-chrome-as-your-default-browser-in-chrome).

faq.question: What is the keyboard shortcut to reopen a closed tab in Chrome on Mac?
faq.answer: Press ⌘ Shift T. Google's keyboard shortcuts page lists it for reopening previously closed tabs in the order they were closed.

faq.question: Can I get back a tab I closed yesterday?
faq.answer: Usually, yes. Open More > History > History and search for the page. Desktop History covers the last 90 days, so a tab from yesterday should appear there unless it was an Incognito page.

faq.question: Why did ⌘ Shift T bring back the wrong tab?
faq.answer: Chrome reopens tabs in the order you closed them, so the most recent one returns first. Press the shortcut again to go further back in the list.

faq.question: Can I reopen a closed Incognito tab?
faq.answer: Incognito pages do not appear in History. Once you close all Incognito windows, the session ends, so save anything you need before you close.

faq.question: Does Chrome have a Reopen Closed Tab item in its Mac menus?
faq.answer: Some third-party guides say yes. Google's help pages do not document that item for Mac, so use the shortcut or the History page instead.

faq.question: What does ⌘ Y do in Chrome on Mac?
faq.answer: It opens the History page in a new tab. Use it when you want to search or scroll a list of pages instead of restoring the last tab.

faq.question: How do I check my Chrome version on Mac?
faq.answer: Choose More > Help > About Google Chrome. Google says a new Chrome update ships about every four weeks, and updates normally install when you close and reopen the browser.

steps.name: Make Chrome the front app
steps.text: Click any part of the Chrome window you were using, or press ⌘ Tab until Chrome is highlighted. The shortcut goes to the app that has focus, so Chrome must be active first.

steps.name: Press ⌘ Shift T
steps.text: Hold Command and Shift, then tap T. Chrome reopens the most recently closed tab. Google documents this shortcut for reopening previously closed tabs.

steps.name: Press again for older tabs
steps.text: Each press reopens one more closed tab, working backward from the last one you closed. Keep pressing until the page you want appears in the tab strip.

steps.name: Open History from the More menu
steps.text: If the shortcut does nothing, click More, the three-dot button at the top right of the Chrome window. Choose History, then History again in the submenu. The History page opens.
steps.tip: ⌘ Y opens History in a new tab directly, so you can skip the menu.

steps.name: Search the History page
steps.text: Type a word from the page title or address into the search box at the top of History. Results cover the last 90 days on desktop. Click the entry to open the page again.

steps.name: Confirm the tab is back
steps.text: Look at the tab strip. The page should appear as a tab. If it is missing, it may be an Incognito page, a chrome:// page, or one older than 90 days. History does not list those.
steps.tip: Type @history in the address bar if you prefer typing to clicking.

shortcuts.action: Open History in a new tab
Move to the next or previous tab
Jump to tabs 1 to 8 by position

troubleshooting.fix: Click the Chrome window first so it is the front app, then press the shortcut again. If no tab comes back, open History with More > History > History and search for the page.
You probably pressed ⌘ Shift N. Close the window with Close at the top left. Incognito pages do not appear in History.

troubleshooting.problem: The page is not in History
troubleshooting.fix: History leaves out Incognito pages, chrome:// pages, pages you deleted, and anything older than 90 days. If the page falls into one of those groups, History cannot show it.

troubleshooting.problem: Your Chrome looks different from these steps
troubleshooting.fix: Update Chrome through More > Help > About Google Chrome. Google says updates normally happen when you close and reopen the browser.

troubleshooting.problem: The menu bar has no Reopen Closed Tab item
troubleshooting.fix: Google's help pages do not document one for Mac. Use ⌘ Shift T or the History page instead.
